items.title: Woman Jumps Into Action After Oct. 7 Terror Attack, Helps Save IDF Soldiers’ Lives
items.author: Billy Hallowell
items.summary: "Our mission is to save lives."
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

An American woman who watched in horror as Hamas’ Oct. 7 attack unfolded felt compelled to take action — and has been saving lives now for nearly three years.

Adi Vaxman, founder and president of Operation Israel, told CBN News she started her organization in an effort to help protect Israeli servicemen and women.

“Our mission is to save lives of the sons and daughters in Israel that are fighting for Israel’s existence and indirectly for, I feel, our existence as the free world, and the Western world, and for American values and Judeo-Christian values,” she said. “So that’s the mission.”

Vaxman, who is Jewish, said she felt called to action by “divine intervention” and signs from God.

“I would say that, on Oct. 7, I always believed in God and my faith was always important to me,” she said. “But I would say that since Oct. 7, it had become not just a lot more important to me, but also a more central grounding force in in my identity because I’ve just been given sign after sign that this is what I’m supposed to do.”

The terror attack left Vaxman in shock, especially considering her personal history. She was a paramedic in Israel during the 1990s and had responded to many terror attacks. Yet what unfolded that day left her stunned as she grappled with unimaginable evil.

“I think it showed the true face of the enemy that we’re all dealing with as as a Judeo-Christian society — as a free society that values life,” she said. “And I think that’s something that every American, every Jew, every Christian, everybody that believes in that way of living needs to understand that we are all fighting as a society that is kind of a bigger, bigger mission.”

Vaxman recalled sitting at home on October 7 watching the horror unfold from afar in America. She recalled feeling as though she would die if she didn’t take action and respond.

“I had a close friend that was locked in her safe room with her kids stuffed inside closets for 26 hours, and we stayed awake and texting with her the whole time, trying to figure out where she was,” she said. “My brother… was rushed to the front lines. He’s a reservist. He’s still serving. He’s still fighting nearly three years later.”

Vaxman said she immediately knew she needed to take action, so she did just that and started sending protective gear to Israeli soldiers to help them amid the newfound battle.

“They didn’t have ceramic vests,” she said of the soldiers. “They didn’t have helmets. They were literally fighting with thousands of terrorists that have endless weapons and endless ammunition with no protection.”

Wanting to solve that problem, Vaxman called a friend who once worked for the Israeli purchasing delegation of the Ministry of Defense. She immediately received information on suppliers of ceramic vests approved by the Israeli Defense Forces and started reaching out.

“I bought everything they had in stock that night,” she said, noting she used personal and business credit cards. “And I had no idea what I was doing in terms of like, how was I going to pay [this] back? I didn’t know.”

The total sum that night was $162,000, yet Vaxman didn’t flinch. She was undeterred by the number and just dove right in, operating on pure survival instinct. Vaxman said she had no time to second guess herself.

“To me, it was do or die, really,” she said. “All I could think about was, ‘Do, do, do or you will die.’ That was my only the only thing in my head was pure survival instinct of, ‘If I don’t do something now I will just collapse into myself and die.’ I have never in my life — and I’ve I’ve had a rough life and I’ve had a lot of painful things happen to me — but I have never in my life felt so helpless and in the amount of pain that I was in that night.”

This was the roots of Operation Israel, an organization Vaxman founded to help soldiers on a more permanent basis. So far, she has raised over $12 million and has touched the lives of 127,000 soldiers, providing defensive gear, equipment, and technologies.

“We never, never ever touch anything offensive,” she said. “We do not provide weapons or anything related to offensive gear. Everything that we do is defensive with the goal of saving lives.”

Vaxman encouraged people to remember that Israel’s military isn’t paid and is all-volunteer — and people begin service at 18 years old, engaging an enemy that has “zero value [for] human life.”

“Everyone in Israel, every person in Israel serves in the army,” she said. “So the soldiers that are serving in the army are split into what’s called mandatory service. They get drafted when they’re 18, and … women serve for two years and men serve for three years minimum. And that’s the mandatory service.”

Vaxman continued, “These are all children. These children don’t deserve to come home in a coffin. They need to come home alive to their families, to their mothers.”

items.title: Ex-Psychic Calls Disney’s Latest Animated Kids’ Movie ‘Really Disturbing’
items.author: Tré Goins-Phillips
items.summary: "We ought to guard our eyes..."
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

Walt Disney Animation Studios just released the first trailer for its upcoming kids’ movie, “Hexed,” and it’s already getting attention.

Jenn Nizza, a former psychic who abandoned the occult after coming to faith in Jesus, described the film as “really disturbing,” arguing in an interview with CBN News that Disney is presenting witchcraft — necromancy, as it’s called in Scripture — “in a really beautiful way.”

“[It] makes me think of Satan masquerading as an angel of light — and that’s really disturbing,” she said.

The movie, releasing in theaters Nov. 25, tells the story of a young teenage girl named Billie, an outcast struggling to fit in. She soon discovers she has magical powers and enters a world called Hexe, where she learns more about witchcraft, spells, and how to channel her supernatural abilities.

While the film seems to suggest there is witchcraft that is morally good, Nizza explains that’s not the case, pointing to biblical admonitions against such practices.

In Deuteronomy 18:10-14 (NLT), it says:

Do not let your people practice fortune-telling, or use sorcery, or interpret omens, or engage in witchcraft, or cast spells, or function as mediums or psychics, or call forth the spirits of the dead. Anyone who does these things is detestable to the LORD. It is because the other nations have done these detestable things that the LORD your God will drive them out ahead of you. But you must be blameless before the LORD your God. The nations you are about to displace consult sorcerers and fortune-tellers, but the LORD your God forbids you to do such things.

There is no morally acceptable witchcraft in God’s sight, according to Scripture.

Although some might argue movies like “Hexed” are just entertainment, Nizza said such films are problematic.

“It’s so important to disregard the aesthetic, because it’s the same evil and it’s the same author of these practices: the devil,” she said, later adding, “This isn’t just a movie. This is implanting and brainwashing the demonic agenda into your minds and into the minds of your children.”

Nizza continued, “We ought to guard our eye gates, our ear gates, and we should be extremely discerning and, honestly, not glorify or celebrate anything that Jesus died on the cross for.”

For her part, Nizza could relate to the main protagonist in “Hexed,” because her interest in witchcraft began at a young age, when she was searching for answers, meaning, and belonging.

“Through that vulnerability … she’s offered this purpose, identity, and power through witchcraft,” she said of Billie’s character. “That is exactly how it started for me when those demonic doors were opened … at age 12 [or] 13.”

And, much like it’s portrayed in “Hexed,” Nizza believed the divination she was practicing was a benefit to herself and those around her because — in her words — she wasn’t “out there trying to curse people for bad things to happen to them.”

“I was doing readings because I believed I really was talking to deceased people, and I had to help them get messages out to their loved ones that were here for … healing, solutions, some sort of peace, some sort of wisdom.”

It wasn’t until her salvation and her abandonment of the occult that she learned she was not, in fact, speaking to dead people.

Instead, she recalled, she was in communication with “demons” who were “masquerading as grandmothers, husbands, wives, and children.”

“I was completely demonically oppressed,” she said. “Of course, I wouldn’t have known that word then — heavy times of depressions, anxieties. … Demonic oppression is a side effect — is what I call it — or a consequence of dealing with the demonic, serving the devil. That’s what I was doing, serving the devil.”

When she was saved, Nizza said, she was indwelled with the Holy Spirit, who led her to study the Bible, where she learned God condemns witchcraft in its entirety.

items.title: God Sees All
items.author: Leslie Koh
items.summary: Michael couldn’t help laughing as Grace hid behind a menu. They were playing a game of hide-and-seek at the table in a café while waiting for the food. The five-year-old thought that if she couldn’t see her father, then he couldn’t see her. It seemed silly at the time, but a
items.content:
📖 Devotional | Our Daily Bread

Michael couldn’t help laughing as Grace hid behind a menu. They were playing a game of hide-and-seek at the table in a café while waiting for the food. The five-year-old thought that if she couldn’t see her father, then he couldn’t see her. It seemed silly at the time, but as Michael reflected on the incident later, he realized it contained an important lesson: Do we believe we can hide our sins from God? Do we think that if we can’t see Him, then He can’t see us?

In Amos 9, this same point is made when God, speaking through the prophet, warns Israel not to think they can escape judgment for their sins. “Though they hide themselves . . . I will hunt them down.” He said, “I will keep my eye on them” (vv. 3-4). Nothing escapes the eyes of the all-seeing, all-knowing God.

But the warning also came with a message of hope. In verses 11-15, God promises restoration: “I will restore David’s fallen shelter—I will repair its broken walls” (v. 11). After suffering the consequences of their sin, God’s people would be restored and given bountiful blessings (vv. 13-15).

Just as God sees our failings, He also sees our repentance, and He is ready to forgive and restore. As we draw comfort from this truth, let’s hold on tightly to the holy and righteous God who is full of mercy and grace.

items.title: Fighting for You
items.author: Karen Pimpo
items.summary: Professional boxer Jim Braddock was known as someone who fought not for riches and fame, but to put food on the table for his family. The movie Cinderella Man chronicles his fairytale-like comeback from a past-his-prime boxer to the world heavyweight champion. While facing extreme poverty during the
items.content:
📖 Devotional | Our Daily Bread

Professional boxer Jim Braddock was known as someone who fought not for riches and fame, but to put food on the table for his family. The movie Cinderella Man chronicles his fairytale-like comeback from a past-his-prime boxer to the world heavyweight champion. While facing extreme poverty during the Great Depression, Jim repeatedly sacrifices his own resources, health, and pride to provide for his children. He’s never intimidated by an opponent and courageously endures pummeling in the ring to keep his family safe.

Jim’s legacy is one of passionate defense of his family. We too, have a passionate defender who has promised to take our place in the ring. When the Israelites faced Pharaoh’s mighty army after their escape from slavery in Egypt, they were terrified and cried out to God. “It would have been better for us to serve the Egyptians than die in the desert!” they foolishly said (Exodus 14:12). But Moses replied in faith: “The Lord will fight for you; you need only to be still” (v. 14). And without any action from the Israelites, their enemies were literally swept away by the sea as God supernaturally ended the battle before it even began.

Sometimes it feels like we’re facing the trials of life or arrows from the enemy, Satan, on our own. But God has promised never to leave us or forsake us (Deuteronomy 31:6). He fights for us; we need only to be still.

items.title: Allie Paige Knows Exactly What Makes Songs Perform. She’s Trying to Ignore It
items.author: Emily Brown
items.summary: Allie Paige has mastered the mug. For the past six months, the indie singer-songwriter has been taking ceramics classes with the goal of filling her kitchen with her own work. She has moved on to bowls. Plates, she said, are still out of reach. It is a small, unhurried way to spend an afternoon for&
items.content:
📖 Culture | Relevant Magazine

Allie Paige has mastered the mug.

For the past six months, the indie singer-songwriter has been taking ceramics classes with the goal of filling her kitchen with her own work. She has moved on to bowls. Plates, she said, are still out of reach.

It is a small, unhurried way to spend an afternoon for an artist who spent her twenties inside church walls, first as the synth player in a worship band, then as the engineer who helped record its debut album out of a four-by-four shed behind her pastor’s house. Paige built a career on that foundation, releasing worship music alongside her own indie project before her sister’s death sent her faith, and her songwriting, somewhere she never expected it to go.

A decade later, Paige has two solo albums behind her, a November tour opening for Jervis Campbell ahead of her, and a relationship with God that no longer resembles the one she grew up performing on stage. She has stepped back from worship leading entirely. She has traded contemporary Christian radio for 1970s Brazilian records. And she has started questioning whether the songs earning her the most streams are the ones she actually wants to be writing.

“I used to be like, I’m a worship leader, and now I’m like, I’m not a worship,” Paige said. “I don’t want to do that. That’s not my calling.”

Paige grew up in classical piano lessons she said she hated, and it was a community college radio production class, taken almost on a whim, that first got her hooked on producing. She started her own project not long after joining the church band, splitting her writing between worship music and everything else until the everything else won out. Her debut album, “Miles,” took three years to finish and came out in 2017. She dropped out of college to tour behind it, worked at a smoothie shop to cover the gap and spent the next decade nannying until she could finally go full time, about two and a half years ago.

The years in between were not gentle.

Not long after “Miles” came out, Paige’s sister died. Another family member later died by suicide. Her parents, she said, have been in crisis for years. Somewhere in the middle of it, a producer held her album hostage in a contract dispute so severe she had to rebuild the entire project, “His World,” from scratch.

“Not everything ends well,” Paige said. “God is present, but he doesn’t stop bad things from happening.”

She is careful to draw a distinction here. Paige still identifies as spiritually connected to God and still writes about him. She has walked away from the version of faith that came prepackaged with easy resolutions, the kind she said she was handed growing up and performed on stage for years. She refuses to write about God as though the story always makes sense.

This refusal has started to cost her something, and she knows it.

Paige has noticed that her best-performing songs follow a formula: pop structure, simple lyrics, spiritual language just digestible enough to travel. She has started catching herself writing toward it, chasing the version of a song that she knows will perform well before she has even finished writing it.

“I’ve realized that my songs that perform the best have a formula,” Paige said. “I started to lean more into that because I’ve gotten to a place where I’m like, I just want to be successful, and I want my numbers up.”

She released a song recently that she almost did not put out because she recognized the formula working in real time as she wrote it. It became one of her top-performing tracks. She is trying to find her way back from that, back to writing the way she did before an audience existed to please, back to what she called the point of art: saying something true and letting people take it or leave it.

The search has led her somewhere unexpected, away from contemporary Christian radio and toward records that never mention church at all. Her last album, His World, was built almost entirely on a diet of Bossa Nova and reggae. She found a 1974 record by the Brazilian musician Jorge Ben Jor with a song about Jesus, sung in imperfect English, that she called one of the most incredible songs she has ever heard. She paired it with a 1960s record by Bossa Nova singer Maria Toledo and kept both on repeat for months, hunting for language about God that did not sound like a worship set.

Her current influences run the same direction. She named Cleo Sol and Natalie Bergman as the two artists shaping her most, both women who write about faith and loss without flattening either one into a single tradition. Bergman wrote her album after losing both of her parents in a car accident. Paige said reading about that process, and hearing what came out of it, felt like a breath of fresh air after years of bedroom pop sameness.

Outside music, Paige’s life has gotten quieter and, by her account, more peaceful. She got married about two years ago and has spent much of that time settling into it. She is deep into ceramics. She has taken up yoga. And after more than a decade of reading almost nothing but theology and self-help, she has started reading fiction again, a habit she said felt indulgent and unproductive until she gave herself permission to do it anyway.

She recently finished “The Book Club for Troublesome Women” and cried. Before that, it was “The Midnight Library,” which she said left her sitting with the uncomfortable question of how many different lives she could still choose to live at 33.

“I feel like I’m rewriting my life in a lot of ways,” Paige said.

The rewriting extends to the music still ahead of her. She has two more live videos coming from “His World,” a November tour opening for Jervis Campbell up the West Coast and through Utah and Colorado, and two more full projects in progress: one with her brother, one under her solo pop name. She has not toured since 2020 and said she can count her live shows since then on one hand.

Paige has little interest in returning to the version of herself who had it figured out. She would rather stay in the questions a little longer and see what comes of it.

items.title: Tuesday, August 25, 2026
items.author: Bishop Robert Barron
items.summary:
Bishop Robert Barron

Friends, in today’s Gospel, Jesus forcefully calls the Pharisees (and us) to change their hearts and behavior.
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Bishop Robert Barron

Daily Reading


First Reading
2 Thessalonians 2:1-3a, 14-17

As to the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ and our being gathered together to him, we beg you, brothers and sisters, not to be quickly shaken in mind or alarmed, either by spirit or by word or by letter, as though from us, to the effect that the day of the Lord is already here. Let no one deceive you in any way; for that day will not come unless the rebellion comes first and the lawless one is revealed, the one destined for destruction.

For this purpose he called you through our proclamation of the good news, so that you may obtain the glory of our Lord Jesus Christ. So then, brothers and sisters, stand firm and hold fast to the traditions that you were taught by us, either by word of mouth or by our letter.

Now may our Lord Jesus Christ himself and God our Father, who loved us and through grace gave us eternal comfort and good hope, comfort your hearts and strengthen them in every good work and word.

Psalm
Psalm 96:10, 11-12, 13

Say among the nations, “The Lord is king!
    The world is firmly established; it shall never be moved.
    He will judge the peoples with equity.”
Let the heavens be glad, and let the earth rejoice;
    let the sea roar, and all that fills it;
     let the field exult, and everything in it.
Then shall all the trees of the forest sing for joy
    before the Lord; for he is coming,
    for he is coming to judge the earth.
He will judge the world with righteousness,
    and the peoples with his truth.

Gospel Reading
Matthew 23:23-26

Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! For you tithe mint, dill, and cummin, and have neglected the weightier matters of the law: justice and mercy and faith. It is these you ought to have practiced without neglecting the others. You blind guides! You strain out a gnat but swallow a camel!

“Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! For you clean the outside of the cup and of the plate, but inside they are full of greed and self-indulgence. You blind Pharisee! First clean the inside of the cup, so that the outside also may become clean.

Reflection

Friends, in today’s Gospel, Jesus forcefully calls the Pharisees (and us) to change their hearts and behavior.

St. Augustine defines sin as incurvatus in se—that means “caved in around oneself.” To be in sin is to be “caved in” around the ego and its narrow concerns. When the Lord says, “Reform your life,” he means move from that old mind and make him the center of your life.

We must know and feel in our bones what is wrong in us; we must look it in the face and acknowledge it with uncompromising honesty. Without this journey into our own inner hell, we will not feel the compunction to shift our way of being and seeing. And we must awaken to what is godlike in us, what is rich and unbroken, what is united with the saving designs of God. Without this clear sense, we will fall into complacency and see metanoia as, at best, a cruel illusion.

items.title: So You’ve Converted—What Now?
items.author: Katy Carl
items.summary:
Katy Carl

Colin Phelps is a young American in Paris who must come to terms with his tendency to deviate transcendence even as he learns to practice a faith that is ever ancient, ever new.
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Katy Carl

Each year at Easter, the Catholic Church eagerly welcomes an influx of new catechumens-turned-mystagogues, many of them younger and just starting out in faith and in life. But by Pentecost we may seem to have forgotten about that moment when we opened wide the doors. We’re back to muddling through, and we seem to expect our converts to get on with it just as we do. What happens to them then? Trevor Cribben Merrill’s new novel The Comforts of Exile tells one possible version of the story through Colin Phelps, a young American in Paris who must come to terms with his tendency to deviate transcendence even as he learns to practice a faith that is ever ancient, ever new.

Although it’s a sequel, this volume stands alone. It’s helpful if readers know what happened to Colin over the course of the prior installment, the campus novel Minor Indignities, but not game-ending if we don’t. Most who finish The Comforts of Exile will have their curiosity piqued and humor primed enough to want to go back and laugh at Colin’s unfailing ability to imagine his way into a better situation only to land himself in a worse one. 

That ability is on full display in Comforts. Here, a freshly graduated and recently baptized-and-confirmed Colin oscillates between Paris’s Left Bank and Manhattan’s gentrifying streets, represented respectively by his two love interests: alluring, chaste Laure and repentant, conflicted Julia, both Catholics yet each holding a different attitude toward the Church’s more difficult teachings. Suspense arises, as it did in the first book, both from the fraught charge of eros and from the comic question to what degree Colin’s propensity for self-sabotage will get in the way of his not inconsiderable talents. 

Many of Colin’s decisions embody a dynamic that anyone who’s undergone any degree of conversion will recognize well: We think that our main problem is in our heads, that if we only put ourselves through enough intellectual change, then our higher thoughts will finally fuel the moral change we want to see in ourselves. Really, though, it’s the other way around. Moral change almost always does precede, and often moral change must precede the intellectual. Wish as we may to change our thoughts, we may not be able to do so until we make the act of will to give up the actions that are getting in the way of our ability to see higher things. 
Word on Fire’s Liturgy of the Hours is Here!
Order Your Set Today

A sidebar here, for the philosophers: This may seem to be going against St. Thomas’s saying that every act of will is preceded by an act of intellect, but it isn’t really. For in order to make the act of the will to change your moral behavior, you do first have to have made the act of the intellect that says, “Changing my moral behavior would be better than not changing it.” That is a separate issue from, say, understanding the truth about how matter and form work in the sacraments. But in practice, someone might not have the freedom of mind to fully understand how matter and form work in the sacraments until he has first successfully said to himself, and followed through on the insight, “You know, it might be a waste of my time and talents to post so many rage-screeds on X” (or “spend so much time doomscrolling,” if shitposting isn’t not your vice), “and I should also probably cut out the day drinking that makes me want to post rage-screeds” (or “the excess caffeine that drives the anxiety that drives the doomscrolling,” if alcohol isn’t your vice). We could multiply examples. The precise fault that gets in the way and the precise truth to be grasped will change according to situation: But the point still holds that, very often, we think we need to think more when really what we need is to do better. Or, as a priest-friend of mine bluntly puts it, “Sin makes you stupid.”

Back to Colin, who reaches this illumination while reading “The Angelic Imagination” and who, to his credit, knows he is too smart to be as stupid as he sometimes is: His relative modesty and self-awareness keep him just this side of humble, even as he stumbles in and out of the rest of the six deadlies, with lust and envy often gaining the upper hand. What there is of Colin’s pride, and there isn’t much, is mostly vanity: the least harmful, because most obvious, kind. (Ordinary pride of arrogance, Augustine’s libido dominandi, easily masks itself as excellence and force of character, while the wretched but all too common pride of timidity masquerades as humility while really being nothing of the sort.)

In fact, Colin is a paradigmatic vaniteux, the sort of character described in René Girard’s Deceit, Desire, and the Novel who “does not want to be anyone’s disciple. He convinces himself that he is thoroughly original”—when, of course, no such thing is the case. This very desire for originality makes the bringing-about of such a character’s religious conversion and social comeuppance—the revelation to himself of his own same-as-everyone-elseness—a particularly rich problem for the comic novelist. Merrill’s complications and conclusions don’t disappoint; Colin, if he is to meet the story’s many demands upon him, will be absolutely required to think less and practice virtue more in a way that could easily provide the impetus for yet a third volume.

Not to spoil the surprise, but Colin undergoes here a classic “novelistic conversion,” which, for Girard, takes place when a central character becomes aware of and disgusted with his vanities. At a higher state of development, the enemy to be fought might not be overt self-aggrandizements, so much as the subtler hesitations, self-preservations, and self-deceptions that not only keep Colin mired in a bad case of staircase wit but, far worse, block him from a fulfilled life in the truth. 

Where Minor Indignities featured the first sort of conversion, Comforts features the second, making Colin a deeper, more substantive, and more interesting character than the rank freshman his earlier readers knew. His French epiphanies are of the pointed but natural type that come to all of us through experience, yet his extreme youth makes it reasonable to believe that he still needs to learn them. This slow process of learning and maturation, perhaps taken for granted or read as implicit by earlier generations, is once again of narrative interest to us in a culture that has all but completely forgotten how to make adults out of adolescents. Colin is in the painful process of psychological molting, shedding the shell of the adolescent to emerge as an actual grown man, and though at times we cringe with and for him, we also cheer him on. Particularly delicious are the novel’s last two lines (don’t jump ahead to them, though; they only make sense in light of the whole), unfolding in their precise choice and sequence of words how the revelation of same-as-everyone-elseness might be cause, not for despair, but for hope.

What makes the tone of the comedy work is Merrill’s thorough understanding of, and compassionate gaze upon, his “bewitched, bothered, and bewildered” protagonist. While not presented as a moral model by any means, Colin is perceived, rather than judged, by the narration. Any judgment delivered is Colin’s own self-judgment and is shown by the turnings of the plot to be entirely justified. In his youthful confusions and earnest if clumsy corrections, Colin stands as an easily comprehensible and perhaps an encouraging figure for those who have recently entered the Church yet still find that their years of (mal)formation in a sick mainstream culture sometimes prove too strong for their good intentions. These new mystagogues don’t need overblown stories of all-but-impossible models to imitate nearly so much they need wise, gentle, humble confessors, such as Colin finds in Père Bayard, who combine serious remonstrance with an abundance of chances to correct course. The young, particularly, don’t need to sit and meditate on their faults—a meditation that life itself will, fortunately and unfortunately, force—nearly so much as they need to fly to the fountain of mercy. Colin’s constant, sincere recourse to the sacraments is his saving grace. It can be ours, too, if we hold fast to it.
